LLM Testing and Evaluation
A practical research guide: choosing models, benchmark files, metrics, formulas, and a reproducible evaluation protocol
Prepared 23 September 2026. “Best” has no universal answer: the best test model and benchmark depend on your task,
language, cost, latency, risk tolerance, and whether the system is a chatbot, RAG application, coding agent, or tool-using
agent.
Executive recommendation
Use a portfolio, not one leaderboard. For a production LLM application, create a private test set from real use cases; score
deterministic requirements with code; add human review for a stratified sample; and use an LLM judge only after calibrating it
against human labels. Public benchmarks are useful for initial model screening, but they cannot prove performance on your
users or documents.
Use case
Recommended primary test assets
Primary outcome
General assistant
HELM + MMLU-Pro/LiveBench + human pairwise preference
Capability breadth, instruction quality
Multi-turn chatbot
MT-Bench-101 + Chatbot Arena-style pairwise human votes
Conversation quality and preference
RAG / document QA
Private grounded QA set + faithfulness, context recall/precision, citation checks
Grounded, useful answers; low hallucination
Code generation
LiveCodeBench + unit tests
Pass@k / executable correctness
Software-engineering agent
SWE-bench Verified or a private issue-replay suite
Resolved issue rate under a fixed environment
Safety / policy
Private red-team prompts + refusal and over-refusal labels
Risk and policy compliance
Indian / multilingual users
Private Hindi/Punjabi-English test set; localized labels
Local-language usefulness and safety
Recommended benchmark files
The following are the most useful open benchmark families. Download data and run the official evaluation harness from each
project’s repository or site, rather than copying leaderboard scores across differing prompts, versions, sampling settings, and
tool configurations.
Benchmark / file family
What it tests
Scoring method / formula
Important limitation
HELM
Broad standardized scenarios and seven dimensions: accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency.
Multi-metric reporting; do not collapse trade-offs into one score without declared weights.
A broad baseline, not a replacement for task-specific tests.
MMLU / MMLU-Pro
Multi-subject knowledge and reasoning. MMLU covers 57 subjects; MMLU-Pro raises reasoning difficulty and uses 10 choices.
Accuracy = correct answers / total questions.
Static datasets can be contaminated; multiple choice is not product behavior.
LiveBench
Frequently refreshed objective tasks across reasoning, math, coding, language, instruction following, data analysis.
Task-specific exact or programmatic scores, aggregated by suite.
Still does not measure your workflow, documents, or users.
MT-Bench / MT-Bench-101
Multi-turn assistant quality; MT-Bench-101 provides fine-grained multi-turn coverage.
LLM-judge or human rating / pairwise win rate.
Judge bias, verbosity bias, and prompt sensitivity require calibration.
Chatbot Arena
Human preference in anonymous side-by-side model comparisons.
Pairwise wins; often summarized with Elo-style ratings.
Population and prompt mix may differ from your target users.
LiveCodeBench
Fresh, contamination-aware coding tasks including generation, repair, execution and output prediction.
Execution/unit-test pass rate; pass@k where multiple samples are generated.
Not equivalent to repository-level engineering tasks.
SWE-bench / SWE-bench Verified
Real GitHub issue resolution across repositories.
Resolved rate = issues whose test suites pass after the agent patch / evaluated issues.
Environment setup, benchmark leakage, and agent scaffolding strongly affect results.
Private golden set
Your actual inputs, retrieved context, expected answer or rubric, metadata and severity.
Deterministic checks + human labels + calibrated LLM judge.
Requires continuous curation and secure handling of data.

Core formulas
Classification or exact-answer accuracy:
Accuracy = (1 / N) Σ■ 1[y■ = ■■]
Precision, recall, and F1 for a positive class:
Precision = TP / (TP + FP); Recall = TP / (TP + FN); F1 = 2 × Precision × Recall / (Precision + Recall)
For code generation with k independently sampled attempts:
pass@k = 1 − C(n − c, k) / C(n, k), where n is the number of generated samples and c is the number that pass; use the
standard estimator only when its assumptions are satisfied.
Pairwise win rate (ties optionally get half credit):
Win rate(A) = (wins(A) + 0.5 × ties(A)) / total comparisons
Elo-style expected probability for model A against B:
P(A beats B) = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B − R_A) / 400))
Calibration via Brier score for predicted confidence p■ and correctness o■ in {0,1}:
Brier = (1 / N) Σ■ (p■ − o■)². Lower is better.
A transparent deployment score can be used only after product owners set weights:
Score = w_q Q + w_s S + w_r R + w_c C + w_l L, with Σw = 1. Q=quality, S=safety, R=reliability, C=normalized cost
efficiency, L=latency score. Report the component scores and weights; do not hide safety failures inside an average.
RAG metrics
For a retrieval-augmented system, measure the retrieval component separately from answer generation. “Faithfulness” asks
whether the answer is supported by the supplied context; “answer relevance” asks whether it answers the question;
contextual recall/precision assess whether retrieved chunks contain needed evidence and avoid irrelevant material. Tools
such as DeepEval expose hallucination, answer relevancy, faithfulness, contextual recall, contextual precision, and
contextual relevancy metrics.
A simple human-audited grounded-answer rate is:
Grounded-answer rate = answers judged both correct and fully supported by retrieved evidence / evaluated answers
For citations, use: Citation precision = supported citations / all citations; Citation recall = claims with at least one supporting
citation / claims requiring citation.
A production testing protocol
1. Define the target behavior. Specify input types, allowed tools, answer format, languages, response time, data sensitivity,
and harms to avoid.
2. Build a versioned private dataset. Each record should include: id, input, expected answer or rubric, supplied/retrieved
context, task tag, language, difficulty, risk severity, and source/date. Include normal, edge, adversarial, multilingual, and
historical failure cases.
3. Split by scenario, not random duplicates. Maintain development, validation, and locked holdout sets. Prevent
near-duplicate documents or templates from leaking across splits.
4. Run deterministic checks first: JSON/schema validity, tool-call validity, citations, PII leakage, policy rules, unit tests,
response length, latency, and cost.
5. Use judges carefully. Have at least two human reviewers label a representative sample; calculate agreement; then
calibrate an LLM judge against those labels. Randomize A/B order in pairwise tests and blind reviewers to model identity.
6. Report uncertainty. For a proportion p on N examples, an approximate 95% interval is p ± 1.96 × sqrt[p(1−p)/N]. Use
bootstrap confidence intervals for more complicated metrics.
7. Gate releases. Example: block deployment if critical-safety pass rate falls below the threshold, if grounded-answer rate
falls by more than a preset margin, or if p95 latency/cost exceeds budget. Track regressions by task slice, not only overall
average.

Example test-set record
id: rag_0142 | input: “What is the refund deadline?” | retrieved_context: policy chunks v2026-09 | expected: “Within 30 days
of purchase, subject to conditions…” | required_citations: [policy-3.2] | rubric: correct deadline=2, correct exceptions=1, no
unsupported claim=2, citation support=1 | tags: RAG, policy, English | severity: high.
Tools and file formats
Recommended portable dataset format: JSONL or CSV. JSONL is usually better for nested retrieved context and multi-turn
conversations. Store prompts, model ID/version, temperature, top-p, seed where available, tool versions, timestamps, raw
output, parsed output, token usage, latency, evaluator version, and scores. This makes a result reproducible.
Framework options: OpenAI Evals is an open-source evaluation framework and registry; LangSmith supports datasets,
target functions, and evaluators for offline/online testing; DeepEval provides research-inspired LLM, RAG, hallucination,
faithfulness, and relevance metrics. Choose based on your stack, privacy constraints, and need for hosted observability.
Key sources and official downloads

 Zheng et al., “Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena” (NeurIPS 2023).
 Li et al., “MT-Bench-101: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Multi-Turn Dialogues” (ACL 2024).
 Wang et al., “MMLU-Pro: A More Robust and Challenging Multi-Task Language Understanding Benchmark” (NeurIPS 2024).
 White et al., “LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Free LLM Benchmark.”
 Jain et al., “LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code.”
 Jimenez et al., “SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?”
 LangSmith documentation: Evaluation concepts and quickstart.
 DeepEval documentation and repository: LLM/RAG metrics including faithfulness and hallucination.
 OpenAI Evals repository and custom-eval documentation.
Interpretation note: no public model, benchmark, or “judge” is globally best. A high score measures performance under that
benchmark’s prompt, protocol, and contamination status. The trustworthy choice is the model that wins on your locked,
representative, safety-weighted evaluation at an acceptable cost and latency.
